claims.text: The initial HEA is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with no detectable brittle secondary phases.
Rapid solidification or other advanced processing produces a uniform BCC or similar single-phase HEA microstructure.
Combined high-temperature and high-stress service exposure induces phase decomposition in the initially single-phase HEA.
Thermal or mechanical exposure produces local compositional inhomogeneities that lower the stability of the original single-phase structure.
Phase decomposition permits the nucleation and growth of secondary intermetallic or Laves phases.
The secondary phases precipitate preferentially at grain boundaries or within the matrix.
The secondary intermetallic or Laves phases are brittle.
Grain-boundary or matrix precipitates act as stress concentrators and sites for crack initiation.
Cracks propagate from the brittle secondary phases under mechanical loading.
The precipitates reduce the alloy's capacity to absorb energy during deformation.
Phase decomposition and precipitation decrease toughness and promote a transition to brittle fracture.
Aged specimens will have lower Charpy impact energy than the unaged baseline.
Aged specimens will have lower crack-propagation resistance than the unaged baseline.
Aged specimens will have increased microhardness because of the secondary precipitates.
Aged specimens will exhibit cleavage facets and intergranular fracture features.
The governing degradation is expected at temperatures potentially at or above 500 degrees Celsius combined with mechanical stresses approaching or exceeding yield strength.
The proposed behavior applies to high-temperature structural service involving sustained or cyclic stress.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis and boundary require combined elevated temperature and high mechanical loading, whereas the intervention and experiment allow thermal or mechanical aging alone. Thus, some permitted tests would not reproduce the exposure claimed to govern the effect.
